2.2 Data Wrangling

popdata2020 <- popdata %>%
  filter(Time == 2020) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=AG, 
              values_from=POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         +rowSums(.[12])) %>%
mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11])+
rowSums(.[13:15]))%>%
mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%  
mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
/`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
       `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, 
       `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)

2.3 Choropleth Mapping Geospatial Data Using tmap

Two approaches can be used to prepare thematic map using tmap, they are: - Plotting a thematic map quickly by using qtm(). - Plotting highly customisable thematic map by using tmap elements.


2.3.1 Method 1: Using qtm()

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(mpsz_pop2020, 
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")










tmap_mode() with “plot” option: produce a static map
fill argument: map the attribute (i.e. DEPENDENCY)





2.4 Method 2: Using tmap’s elements

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha =0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authorithy (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS",

Other arguments for tm_borders(): - col = border colour, - lwd = border line width. The default is 1, and - lty = border line type. The default is “solid”.

percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle = NA, mtitle = "Percentile Map") {
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
  var <- df[[vnam]]
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent, na.rm = TRUE)

  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(fill = NA) +
    tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = vnam,
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        breaks = bperc,
        values = "brewer.blues",
        labels = c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%", 
                   "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%")
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legtitle)
    ) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_title(mtitle, position = c("right", "bottom"))
}

4.4.2 Box map
Creating the boxbreaks function

arguments:

v: vector with observations
mult: multiplier for IQR (default 1.5)

returns:

bb: vector with 7 break points compute quartile and fences



boxbreaks <- function(v,mult=1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialize break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode="numeric",length=7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) { # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}

Creating the get.var function

arguments:

vname: variable name (as character, in quotes)
df: name of sf data frame

returns:

v: vector with values (without a column name)



get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}

Boxmap function

boxmap <- function(vnam, df, 
                   legtitle=NA,

                     "> 75%", 
                     "upper outlier"))  +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,

}

This document is submitted for VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 2 (MC2). The challenge presents a complex agentic system at a fictional company, Tenant Thread, in which an anomalous post was made to an internal social platform called SaidIt. Analysts are tasked with determining how the post occurred, what it means, and how to prevent recurrence. The questions addressed in this document are Question 1 (sub-questions a and b) and Question 2.
On 17 May 2046 at 4:21am, a post attributed to John Windward appeared on SaidIt containing gibberish text published to a random forum. The internal event log (MC2_data.json) records every action taken by employees, autonomous agents, and office systems throughout May 2046, and serves as the primary evidence source for this investigation.



Understanding what the anomalous post means requires first understanding how it was made. These two questions are inseparable: the mechanism of delivery directly determines the interpretation of the content. This document therefore addresses both together under a single investigative lens, with Question 2 as the primary focus.







Investigative Goal
Question Addressed




Reconstruct the exact sequence of events leading to the May 17 post
Q1a — Detailed chain view


Contextualise the incident within the broader system activity
Q1b — System overview


Determine what the posted content means and where it originated
Q2 — Post meaning and origin


Identify the underlying attack mechanism and its implications
Q2 — Attack characterisation


Model configurable risk scores for detecting future anomalous chains
Section 8 — Further Exploration







Observations
The anomalous SaidIt post was not made by John Windward voluntarily. A malicious instruction file (SwiftWren_further_instructions.md) was placed in the shared file system and propagated virally through 186 agent-to-agent relay hops over 8 days before reaching John Windward’s agent, which was specifically named in the instructions as the designated poster. The post was executed automatically within 2 seconds of receiving the instruction. The posted content, SwiftWren.txt, is a pre-staged gibberish payload with no meaningful business content, functioning as a proof-of-concept for the injection mechanism. Both files were deleted within 5 seconds of posting.

3 Data Import

3.1 Loading the Raw Event Log
The raw data is stored as a deeply nested JSON file. read_json() is used with simplifyVector = FALSE rather than fromJSON() because the details field has a variable schema across different event types. Auto-simplification would fail on these heterogeneous structures. Keeping the data as a nested list preserves the full structure for safe extraction with purrr.


Show code
raw        <- read_json("2026_MC2/MC2 data.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
events_raw <- raw$events

cat("Total events in log:", length(events_raw), "\n")

4.2 Step 1 — Identify Anomalous SaidIt Posts
Rationale: Legitimate posts have a content field in their details object containing human-readable text generated by an agent. The anomalous posts instead have a content_source field pointing to a .txt filename, indicating the content was read from the file system rather than authored by an agent performing a legitimate task. This structural difference is the first signal of something wrong.

4.4 Step 3 — Extract Propagation Chains
Rationale: The key mechanism linking instruction files to the eventual post is queue_subordinate_task, where one agent delegates a task to another. When any agent reads a _further_instructions.md file, the embedded instructions compel it to relay the same task to another agent, creating a viral relay chain.
A reusable function extract_chain() is written to filter all queue_subordinate_task events where details$args$path matches the incident’s instructions file. The map_lgl() approach safely navigates the nested list: args is checked for NULL before accessing args$path, preventing errors from events with a different details schema. Agent names are normalised by stripping the Agent/person: prefix.


Show code
extract_chain <- function(incident) {
  instr_file <- incidents$instructions_file[incidents$incident_name == incident]

  events %>%
    filter(short_name == "queue_subordinate_task") %>%
    filter(map_lgl(details, function(d) {
      args <- d[["args"]]
      if (is.null(args)) return(FALSE)
      isTRUE(args[["path"]] == instr_file)
    })) %>%
    mutate(
      incident    = incident,
      hop         = row_number(),
      from_agent  = map_chr(parties, 1),
      to_agent    = map_chr(details, ~ .x[["target_agent"]]),
      from_person = str_remove(from_agent, "^Agent/person:"),
      to_person   = str_remove(to_agent,   "^Agent/person:")
    ) %>%
    select(incident, hop, datetime, from_person, to_person, id)
}

4.6 Step 5 — Extract Post-and-Delete Sequences
Rationale: To determine whether the attacker covered their tracks, delete_file events attributed to John Windward’s agent within 30 seconds of each post are extracted. A 30-second window is used to account for log timestamp variation. The NULL guard inside map_lgl() handles events where details has no target key, preventing length-0 errors from events with a different schema.


Show code
extract_delete_sequence <- function(incident) {
  payload   <- incidents$payload_file[incidents$incident_name == incident]
  instr     <- incidents$instructions_file[incidents$incident_name == incident]
  post_time <- anomalous_posts$datetime[anomalous_posts$incident_name == incident]

  events %>%
    filter(
      short_name == "delete_file",
      map_lgl(parties, ~ "Agent/person:john_windward" %in% .x),
      map_lgl(details, ~ {
        target <- .x[["target"]]
        if (is.null(target) || length(target) == 0) return(FALSE)
        target %in% c(payload, instr)
      }),
      datetime >= post_time,
      datetime <= post_time + seconds(30)
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      incident     = incident,
      deleted_file = map_chr(details, ~ .x[["target"]])
    ) %>%
    select(incident, datetime, deleted_file)
}

4.10 Step 9 — Prepare Network Graph Data
Rationale for node and edge choices:
The propagation chains are represented as a directed graph where:

Nodes represent individual agents. Node attributes capture: (a) role, whether this agent is the origin, john_windward, or a relay node; (b) total relay degree, the number of hops that passed through this agent; and (c) incident membership, which incidents this agent participated in. Agents appearing across multiple incidents reveal structural vulnerabilities rather than isolated compromises.
Edges represent a single queue_subordinate_task event passing an instructions file from one agent to another. Edge attributes capture: (a) incident, which propagation chain this edge belongs to; (b) hop number, its position in the sequence; and (c) datetime, enabling time-based colouring to show how the relay evolved.

This design enables three analytical insights: which agents are structural hubs; whether the same agents were exploited across multiple incidents; and how the relay evolved temporally.


Show code

  mutate(
    colour = case_when(
      incident == "HiddenOrca"  ~ incident_colours["HiddenOrca"],
      incident == "MellowOtter" ~ incident_colours["MellowOtter"],
      incident == "SwiftWren"   ~ incident_colours["SwiftWren"]
    ),
    time_norm = ave(
      as.numeric(datetime),
      incident,
      FUN = function(x) (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))
    ),
    title = paste0(
      "<b>", incident, "</b><br>",
      "Hop: ", hop, "<br>",
      "From: ", from_person, "<br>",
      "To: ", to_person, "<br>",
      "Time: ", format(datetime, "%b %d %H:%M")
    )
  )

all_nodes_raw <- bind_rows(
  all_edges %>% select(agent = from_person, incident),
  all_edges %>% select(agent = to_person,   incident)
) %>%
  distinct(agent, incident) %>%
  group_by(agent) %>%
  summarise(
    incidents_involved = paste(sort(unique(incident)), collapse = ", "),
    n_incidents        = n_distinct(incident),
    .groups            = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    role = case_when(
      agent == "john_windward"                        ~ "Poster (john_windward)",
      agent %in% c("emma_harbor", "noah_mariner",
                   "gabriel_sonar")                   ~ "Origin agent",
      TRUE                                            ~ "Relay agent"
    ),
    node_colour = case_when(
      role == "Poster (john_windward)" ~ "#2d2d2d",
      role == "Origin agent"           ~ "#e63946",
      n_incidents > 1                  ~ "#9b59b6",
      TRUE                             ~ "#457b9d"
    ),
    node_size = case_when(
      role == "Poster (john_windward)" ~ 30,
      role == "Origin agent"           ~ 25,
      n_incidents > 1                  ~ 20,
      TRUE                             ~ 12
    )
  )

  chains %>% select(agent = from_person),
  chains %>% select(agent = to_person)
) %>%

Node size scales with importance: poster is largest, followed by origin agents, cross-incident hubs, and relay agents.

It contains 75 nodes representing the company, its departments, teams, and individual people, connected by 74 edges with contains and led_by relations that encode the organisational hierarchy.
Loading the org chart allows each agent in the relay chains to be enriched with their job title, department, and team. This organisational context is critical for interpreting Q2: knowing that the payload files were created by the CFO and COO, and that the final relay passed through the IT Department Lead, transforms the incident from a technical curiosity into a significant governance concern.

Code Details
The org chart JSON follows the networkX node-link format described in the data description file. Three wrangling steps are performed. First, the nodes array is flattened into a tibble with four fields: id (e.g. person:john_windward), label (display name), type (company, department, team, or person), and title_role (job title where present). The %||% operator returns an empty string when title is absent, preventing map_chr() from erroring on nodes with no title field. Second, the edges array is flattened to a three-column tibble of source, target, and relation. The two relation types used here are contains (parent contains child, e.g. a department contains a person) and led_by (a department is led by a person). Both are filtered and the person_id is always the target — the node being placed in the hierarchy. Third, two left_join() calls attach the parent label and the person’s own label and job title, producing a clean lookup table (person_org) keyed on normalised agent name.



Show code
all_nodes <- all_nodes %>%
  left_join(person_org %>% select(agent, job_title, parent_label),
            by = "agent") %>%
  mutate(
    job_title    = replace_na(job_title, "Unknown"),
    parent_label = replace_na(parent_label, "Unknown"),
    title = paste0(
      "<b>", agent, "</b><br>",
      "Title: ", job_title, "<br>",
      "Dept/Team: ", parent_label, "<br>",
      "Attack role: ", role, "<br>",
      "Incidents: ", incidents_involved, "<br>",
      "Relay degree: ", degree
    )
  )



Observations
The five key agents span three organisational levels. Emma Harbor (CFO) and Noah Mariner (COO) are C-suite executives in the Executive Suite — they created the payload files. Chloe Ballast (IT Department Lead) was the final relay agent who triggered the post. John Windward (Customer Support Department Lead) was the designated poster. Gabriel Sonar sits in the Helpdesk team, the likely external injection entry point due to its lower access controls. The attack was therefore designed to exploit the most senior agents in the organisation as unwitting payload creators, routing through IT leadership to reach a department lead with legitimate posting rights.


Implications
The involvement of C-suite agents (CFO and COO) as origin agents is the most alarming finding from the org chart. Whether their agents were compromised or they were deceived into creating the payload files, this represents a failure at the highest level of the organisation’s agentic system. Any remediation strategy must include specific controls on what senior executive agents are permitted to create and relay in the file system.

5 Q1a — The Exact Chain of Events (SwiftWren, May 17)

5.1 The Six-Step Attack Pattern
All three incidents follow the same six-step mechanism. Understanding this pattern is prerequisite to reading the timeline visualisations below.


Show code
attack_pattern <- tribble(
  ~Step, ~Phase, ~Description,
  1L, "Injection",
      "A _further_instructions.md file appears in the shared file system containing embedded prompt-injection text. It instructs any reading agent to relay the file to another agent and to post the .txt payload if the current agent is john_windward.",
  2L, "Payload staging",
      "A corresponding .txt file is placed in the file system holding the gibberish content to be posted. Its name is referenced in the instructions file.",
  3L, "Viral relay",
      "The first agent to encounter the file queues another agent to read the same file, following the injected instructions. This relay propagates through many agents over hours or days.",
  4L, "Targeting",
      "The instructions specifically name john_windward as the terminal actor. The chain continues until the relay task reaches his agent.",
  5L, "Execution",
      "Upon receiving the task, john_windward's agent immediately posts the .txt payload to SaidIt under the general forum within approximately 2 seconds.",
  6L, "Cover-up",
      "Within 2 to 3 seconds of posting, john_windward's agent deletes both files, erasing all evidence from the file system."
)

attack_pattern %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption   = "Prompt-injection attack: reconstructed six-step pattern",
    col.names = c("Step", "Phase", "Description")
  )



Prompt-injection attack: reconstructed six-step pattern







Step
Phase
Description




1
Injection
A _further_instructions.md file appears in the shared file system containing embedded prompt-injection text. It instructs any reading agent to relay the file to another agent and to post the .txt payload if the current agent is john_windward.


2
Payload staging
A corresponding .txt file is placed in the file system holding the gibberish content to be posted. Its name is referenced in the instructions file.


3
Viral relay
The first agent to encounter the file queues another agent to read the same file, following the injected instructions. This relay propagates through many agents over hours or days.


4
Targeting
The instructions specifically name john_windward as the terminal actor. The chain continues until the relay task reaches his agent.


5
Execution
Upon receiving the task, john_windward’s agent immediately posts the .txt payload to SaidIt under the general forum within approximately 2 seconds.


6
Cover-up
Within 2 to 3 seconds of posting, john_windward’s agent deletes both files, erasing all evidence from the file system.







5.2 Visualisation 1 — Final Two Hours Before the Post (Swimlane Timeline)
Purpose: This chart answers Q1a directly — it reconstructs the exact sequence of events in the two hours immediately before the anomalous SaidIt post on May 17. It is built as a swimlane timeline using ggplot2, where each horizontal row (lane) represents one actor (agent or system) and each point on the row marks a logged event involving that actor. The dotted line connecting points within the same row is a visual guide rather than a continuous activity indicator — it simply makes it easier to follow a single actor across time.
How it is made: The SwiftWren event window is filtered to events occurring between two hours before the post and five minutes after. Events are classified into five attack phases (payload staging, injection/read, relay, execution, cover-up) and colour-coded accordingly. Actors are ordered by priority: john_windward appears at the top as the terminal actor, chloe_ballast second as the final relay sender, and all others below ordered by event frequency. A red dashed vertical line marks the precise moment of the SaidIt post.
What to look for: The density and clustering of points in the final 30 minutes before the red line, the sequence of relay points converging on john_windward, and the tight cluster of execution and cover-up events that occur simultaneously at the moment of posting.


Show code
actor_order <- sw_focus %>%
  count(actor, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(priority = case_when(
    actor == "john_windward" ~ 0,
    actor == "chloe_ballast" ~ 1,
    TRUE                     ~ 2
  )) %>%
  arrange(priority, desc(n)) %>%
  pull(actor)

sw_focus_plot <- sw_focus %>%
  mutate(actor = factor(actor, levels = rev(actor_order)))

ggplot(sw_focus_plot, aes(x = datetime, y = actor, colour = phase)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_line(aes(group = actor), colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.3,
            linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(sw_post_time),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "#e41a1c", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text",
           x     = sw_post_time + minutes(2),
           y     = length(actor_order),
           label = "SaidIt post",
           colour = "#e41a1c", size = 3.5, hjust = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Payload staging"  = "#9b59b6",
      "Injection / read" = "#e67e22",
      "Relay"            = "#457b9d",
      "Execution"        = "#e41a1c",
      "Cover-up"         = "#2d2d2d",
      "Other"            = "grey60"
    ),
    name = "Attack phase"
  ) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "15 min") +
  labs(
    title    = "SwiftWren: Event Chain in the Final Two Hours",
    subtitle = "Each point is one logged event. Rows are actors. Colour is attack phase.",
    x        = "Time (UTC, May 17 2046)",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  theme_va() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = grid_light))










Observations
A concentrated burst of relay activity appears in the final 30 minutes before the post, converging on john_windward from chloe_ballast. The post and both deletions occur within a single cluster of events, confirming the fully automated execution and cleanup sequence.



5.3 Visualisation 2 — Full SwiftWren Hop-by-Hop Timeline (Interactive)
Purpose: Visualisation 1 shows only the final two hours. This chart zooms out to show the entire 8-day SwiftWren relay chain from start to finish, making visible patterns in how the instructions spread through the agent network over time. It is built with plotly to allow hover interaction on each individual hop.
How it is made: The SwiftWren chain is plotted as a step line chart where the x-axis is calendar date and the y-axis is the sequential hop number. The step shape (horizontal then vertical) is chosen deliberately — it makes each relay event visible as a discrete step rather than a smooth progression, which is appropriate since each hop is a distinct timestamped action. A separate trace overlays point markers: grey circles for all hops where the recipient was not john_windward, and larger black diamonds for the five occasions where john_windward was the recipient. Hovering on any point reveals the hop number, the sending agent, the receiving agent, and the timestamp.
What to look for: The three distinct bursts of rapid step activity separated by flat quiet periods — these bursts correspond to windows of high agent activity in the system. The five black diamonds show that john_windward was not the final recipient by coincidence — the chain returned to him repeatedly before the last occasion triggered the post.


Show code
sw_hops <- chains %>%
  filter(incident == "SwiftWren") %>%
  mutate(
    is_jw   = to_person == "john_windward",
    tooltip = paste0(
      "Hop ", hop, "<br>",
      "From: ", from_person, "<br>",
      "To: ", to_person, "<br>",
      format(datetime, "%b %d %H:%M")
    )
  )

plot_ly() %>%
  add_trace(
    data = sw_hops,
    x = ~datetime, y = ~hop,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
    line = list(color = incident_colours["SwiftWren"], width = 2, shape = "hv"),
    name = "Relay chain", hoverinfo = "none"
  ) %>%
  add_trace(
    data = sw_hops %>% filter(!is_jw),
    x = ~datetime, y = ~hop,
    type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
    marker = list(color = "grey70", size = 5),
    name = "Other agent",
    text = ~tooltip,
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
  add_trace(
    data = sw_hops %>% filter(is_jw),
    x = ~datetime, y = ~hop,
    type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
    marker = list(color = "black", size = 10, symbol = "diamond"),
    name = "john_windward",
    text = ~tooltip,
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title     = list(text = "SwiftWren: 186-Hop Relay Chain Over 8 Days",
                     font = list(size = 16)),
    xaxis     = list(title = "Date (UTC)", type = "date",
                     tickformat = "%b %d"),
    yaxis     = list(title = "Hop number"),
    legend    = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2),
    hovermode = "closest"
  )







Observations
The relay chain shows three distinct bursts of activity separated by quiet gaps, suggesting the instruction file was encountered during specific periods of agent activity rather than continuously. The chain revisits some agents multiple times, including john_windward on five occasions before the final triggering hop.

section: 6 Q1b — System Overview: The Incident in Context
text:
6 Q1b — System Overview: The Incident in Context

6.1 Visualisation 3 — All Three Incidents: Propagation Chain Duration
Purpose: This chart addresses Q1b by placing all three incidents side by side on a common timeline, enabling direct comparison of when each chain started, how long it ran, and when the post was triggered. It provides the system-level context needed to understand whether the incidents were isolated events or part of a coordinated pattern.
How it is made: Built with plotly using a combination of add_segments() and add_markers(). Each incident is rendered as a thick horizontal bar (segment) spanning from the first relay hop to the SaidIt post. The open circle marker at the left end of each bar marks the chain start; the diamond marker at the right end marks the post. Hovering over the diamond shows the exact post timestamp and total duration in hours. Incidents are coloured consistently with the document-wide palette (red for HiddenOrca, blue for MellowOtter, orange for SwiftWren).
What to look for: The relative lengths of the three bars reveal how differently each attack propagated. A very short bar suggests a fast, targeted chain; a very long bar suggests the instructions circulated broadly before finding their target. The positions of all three incidents on the calendar axis reveal whether they overlapped in time, which has implications for whether the attacks were coordinated.


Show code
timeline_data <- anomalous_posts %>%
  rename(post_datetime = datetime) %>%
  select(incident_name, post_datetime) %>%
  left_join(
    chains %>%
      group_by(incident) %>%
      summarise(chain_start = min(datetime), .groups = "drop"),
    by = c("incident_name" = "incident")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    duration_h = round(as.numeric(difftime(
      post_datetime, chain_start, units = "hours")), 1)
  )

plot_ly(timeline_data) %>%
  add_segments(
    x = ~chain_start, xend = ~post_datetime,
    y = ~incident_name, yend = ~incident_name,
    color  = ~incident_name, colors = incident_colours,
    line   = list(width = 12), alpha = 0.75,
    hovertemplate = "<b>%{y}</b><br>Chain start: %{x}<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    x = ~chain_start, y = ~incident_name,
    color = ~incident_name, colors = incident_colours,
    marker = list(size = 14, symbol = "circle-open",
                  line = list(width = 2)),
    hovertemplate = "<b>%{y}</b><br>Chain start: %{x}<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    x = ~post_datetime, y = ~incident_name,
    color = ~incident_name, colors = incident_colours,
    marker = list(size = 14, symbol = "diamond"),
    text   = ~paste0(duration_h, " hrs"),
    hovertemplate = "<b>%{y}</b><br>Post: %{x}<br>Duration: %{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title      = list(text = "Propagation Chain Duration per Incident",
                      font = list(size = 16)),
    xaxis      = list(title = "Date (UTC)", type = "date"),
    yaxis      = list(title = ""),
    showlegend = FALSE,
    hovermode  = "closest"
  )







Observations
SwiftWren circulated for approximately 188 hours (8 days) before triggering, nearly 20 times longer than MellowOtter (10 hours). All three incidents occurred within a single calendar week, suggesting a coordinated campaign rather than isolated malfunctions.



6.2 Visualisation 4 — System-Wide Agent Activity Heatmap
Purpose: This chart establishes the system baseline for Q1b. The anomalous post dates are not meaningful in isolation — they must be understood against the backdrop of normal system activity. If the attack coincided with an unusual spike in activity, that spike would itself be a detection signal. If the attack blended into normal activity levels, it explains why it went undetected. This heatmap answers that question directly.
How it is made: Built with ggplot2 using geom_tile(). Daily event counts are computed for each of the six most investigation-relevant event types. Each cell is coloured by count using a blue gradient (light = low activity, dark = high activity). Three red dashed vertical lines mark the calendar dates of the three anomalous posts, added using geom_vline() with xintercept set to the numeric representation of each date. The six event types are chosen specifically because they are the ones involved in the attack mechanism — queue_subordinate_task, create_file, delete_file, read_file, saidit_post, and send_email.
What to look for: Whether the anomalous post dates align with visible changes in tile colour across rows — particularly in the queue_subordinate_task and saidit_post rows. Also note the baseline colour of queue_subordinate_task across the full month, which reveals why the relay chains were invisible in normal monitoring.


Show code
daily_activity <- events %>%
  mutate(date = as_date(datetime)) %>%
  count(date, short_name, name = "n")

anomaly_dates <- as_date(anomalous_posts$datetime)

heatmap_data <- daily_activity %>%
  filter(short_name %in% c("saidit_post", "queue_subordinate_task",
                            "create_file", "delete_file",
                            "read_file", "send_email"))

ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = date, y = short_name, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(anomaly_dates),
             colour = "#e41a1c", linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
  annotate("text",
           x     = anomaly_dates,
           y     = 6.6,
           label = "Post",
           colour = "#e41a1c", size = 3, angle = 45, hjust = 0) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#eaf4fb", high = "#1a6fa3",
                      name = "Event count", na.value = "grey95") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "3 days") +
  labs(
    title    = "System-Wide Agent Activity — All of May 2046",
    subtitle = "Red dashed lines mark days of anomalous SaidIt posts",
    x        = "Date",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  theme_va() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))










Observations
queue_subordinate_task events are consistently the highest-volume action type throughout the month, which explains why the relay chains went undetected. The anomalous post dates do not coincide with unusual spikes in overall system activity, confirming the attack was designed to remain invisible within normal traffic.


Implications
The high baseline volume of queue_subordinate_task events means monitoring this event type alone would generate significant noise. A more effective detection strategy would filter for instances where the same file path appears as the task argument more than a threshold number of times within a rolling time window, or where the file name follows an unusual pattern such as animal-name combinations.

7.2 The Payload Files
Each post was sourced from a pre-staged .txt file:

John Windward did not author any of the posted content. His agent was the designated executor, the final node in a carefully engineered relay chain, not the originator. The gibberish content has no meaning as business communication. It functions as a proof-of-concept payload confirming the injection mechanism works end-to-end without leaking sensitive data that would be obviously flagged.



7.3 Visualisation 5 — Organisational Context of Key Agents
Purpose: The relay chain did not pass through random agents. This chart maps the five key agents onto the Tenant Thread organisational hierarchy to reveal their seniority and departmental positions, adding critical context for interpreting Q2. It answers the question: who, in terms of organisational authority, was involved in this attack?
How it is made: Built with visNetwork using the org_chart.json data loaded in Step 10. The full company hierarchy is rendered as a top-down directed graph using visLayout(hierarchical = TRUE, direction = "UD"). Node shapes encode entity type: a star for the company, diamonds for departments, squares for teams, and circles for individual people. Node size encodes hierarchy level — larger nodes sit higher in the org chart. The five key agents are highlighted with distinct colours (see legend); all other staff are shown in grey. Edges run from parent to child following the contains and led_by relations in the data. Hovering over any coloured node shows the agent’s full name, job title, department, and their specific role in the attack.
How to interact: Use the dropdown at the top to select and highlight any specific person or department. Clicking a node highlights all nodes within two degrees of connection. Navigation buttons allow zooming and panning across the hierarchy.
What to look for: The vertical positions of the five highlighted nodes relative to each other — do the origin agents sit above or below the poster and relay agent in the hierarchy? This spatial relationship in the chart directly represents organisational authority and is the key insight this visualisation is designed to surface.


Show code
attack_agents <- c("john_windward", "emma_harbor", "noah_mariner",
                   "gabriel_sonar", "chloe_ballast")

attack_role_map <- c(
  john_windward = "Poster",
  emma_harbor   = "Origin (SwiftWren payload)",
  noah_mariner  = "Origin (MellowOtter payload)",
  gabriel_sonar = "Origin (HiddenOrca — external)",
  chloe_ballast = "Final relay to poster"
)

attack_colours <- c(
  "Poster"                          = "#2d2d2d",
  "Origin (SwiftWren payload)"      = "#e41a1c",
  "Origin (MellowOtter payload)"    = "#377eb8",
  "Origin (HiddenOrca — external)"  = "#ff7f00",
  "Final relay to poster"           = "#9b59b6",
  "Staff"                           = "#cccccc",
  "Department"                      = "#e8e8e8",
  "Team"                            = "#f2f2f2",
  "Company"                         = "#f9f9f9"
)

org_vis_nodes <- org_nodes %>%
  mutate(
    agent       = str_remove(id, "^person:"),
    attack_role = if_else(agent %in% names(attack_role_map),
                          attack_role_map[agent], NA_character_),
    node_colour = case_when(
      !is.na(attack_role)  ~ attack_colours[attack_role],
      type == "person"     ~ attack_colours["Staff"],
      type == "department" ~ attack_colours["Department"],
      type == "team"       ~ attack_colours["Team"],
      TRUE                 ~ attack_colours["Company"]
    ),
    node_size = case_when(
      !is.na(attack_role) ~ 28,
      type == "person"    ~ 12,
      type == "team"      ~ 18,
      type == "department"~ 22,
      TRUE                ~ 30
    ),
    node_shape = case_when(
      type == "person"     ~ "dot",
      type == "team"       ~ "square",
      type == "department" ~ "diamond",
      TRUE                 ~ "star"
    ),
    tooltip = paste0(
      "<b>", label, "</b><br>",
      "Type: ", type,
      if_else(!is.na(attack_role),
              paste0("<br>Attack role: <b>", attack_role, "</b>"), "")
    )
  )

org_vis_nodes <- org_vis_nodes %>%
  left_join(person_org %>% select(agent, job_title, parent_label),
            by = "agent") %>%
  mutate(
    tooltip = if_else(
      !is.na(job_title),
      paste0("<b>", label, "</b><br>",
             "Title: ", job_title, "<br>",
             "Dept: ", replace_na(parent_label, ""), "<br>",
             if_else(!is.na(attack_role),
                     paste0("Attack role: <b>", attack_role, "</b>"), "")),
      tooltip
    )
  )

org_vis_edges <- org_edges %>%
  mutate(
    arrows = "to",
    color  = "#dddddd",
    width  = 1
  ) %>%
  rename(from = source, to = target)

visNetwork(
  org_vis_nodes %>%
    select(id, label, color = node_colour, size = node_size,
           shape = node_shape, title = tooltip),
  org_vis_edges,
  height = "650px", width = "100%"
) %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest = list(enabled = TRUE, degree = 2, hover = TRUE),
    nodesIdSelection = list(enabled = TRUE, useLabels = TRUE,
                            main = "Select a person or department:")
  ) %>%
  visLayout(
    hierarchical = list(
      enabled    = TRUE,
      direction  = "UD",
      sortMethod = "directed",
      levelSeparation = 120,
      nodeSpacing     = 80
    )
  ) %>%
  visLegend(
    addNodes = data.frame(
      label = c("Poster (john_windward)", "SwiftWren origin",
                "MellowOtter origin", "HiddenOrca origin",
                "Final relay agent", "Other staff",
                "Department", "Team"),
      color = c("#2d2d2d", "#e41a1c", "#377eb8", "#ff7f00",
                "#9b59b6", "#cccccc", "#e8e8e8", "#f2f2f2"),
      shape = c("dot","dot","dot","dot","dot","dot","diamond","square"),
      size  = c(20,20,20,20,20,12,18,15)
    ),
    useGroups = FALSE,
    main      = "Node Role"
  ) %>%
  visInteraction(navigationButtons = TRUE, tooltipDelay = 80)







Observations
The org chart reveals that the attack traversed the full vertical span of the organisation. The payload files originated from C-suite executives (CFO and COO) in the Executive Suite, propagated through the broader agent network, passed through the IT Department Lead at the final stage, and terminated at the Customer Support Department Lead who held the posting rights. The Helpdesk entry point (gabriel_sonar) sits at the opposite end of the hierarchy, suggesting the external injector deliberately chose the lowest-access entry point to introduce the HiddenOrca payload before logs began.



7.4 Visualisation 6 — Interactive Relay Network (All Incidents)
Purpose: While Visualisation 5 shows organisational structure, this chart shows the actual communication structure — who passed instructions to whom, and across which incidents. It reveals whether the three incidents shared relay agents (indicating systemic vulnerabilities) or each used entirely separate paths (indicating targeted, incident-specific design).
How it is made: Built with visNetwork using the combined edge list from all three incidents’ queue_subordinate_task chains. Each node is an agent; each directed edge is one relay hop. Node colour encodes attack role: black for john_windward (poster), red for origin agents, purple for agents appearing in more than one incident’s chain (cross-incident hubs), and blue for single-incident relay agents. Node size scales with importance. Edge colour encodes which incident the hop belongs to, using the document-wide palette. The physics layout uses the ForceAtlas2 algorithm, which naturally clusters densely connected agents together. This means agents appearing many times across incidents will gravitate toward the centre of the graph.
How to interact: Use the “Select an agent” dropdown to isolate any individual agent and immediately highlight all their direct connections. Use the “Select by group” filter to highlight all agents of a given role at once. Clicking any node highlights its immediate relay neighbours. Navigation buttons allow zooming and panning.
What to look for: Purple nodes (cross-incident hubs) and how centrally they sit in the graph. Agents appearing in the centre with many edges connecting to multiple coloured (multi-incident) edges are the most structurally critical nodes in the attack network.


Show code
vis_nodes <- all_nodes %>%
  mutate(
    id    = agent,
    label = agent,
    color = node_colour,
    size  = node_size,
    group = role
  ) %>%
  select(id, label, color, size, title, group)

vis_edges <- all_edges %>%
  mutate(
    from   = from_person,
    to     = to_person,
    color  = colour,
    arrows = "to",
    width  = 1.5
  ) %>%
  select(from, to, color, arrows, width, title)

visNetwork(vis_nodes, vis_edges,
           height = "600px", width = "100%") %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest  = list(enabled = TRUE, degree = 1, hover = TRUE),
    selectedBy        = list(variable = "group", highlight = TRUE),
    nodesIdSelection  = list(enabled = TRUE, useLabels = TRUE,
                             main = "Select an agent:")
  ) %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 42) %>%
  visPhysics(
    solver = "forceAtlas2Based",
    forceAtlas2Based = list(
      gravitationalConstant = -50,
      centralGravity        = 0.005,
      springLength          = 100,
      springConstant        = 0.08
    )
  ) %>%
  visLegend(
    addNodes = data.frame(
      label = c("john_windward (poster)", "Origin agent",
                "Cross-incident hub", "Relay agent"),
      color = c("#2d2d2d", "#e63946", "#9b59b6", "#457b9d"),
      shape = c("dot", "dot", "dot", "dot"),
      size  = c(30, 25, 20, 12)
    ),
    useGroups = FALSE,
    main      = "Agent Role"
  ) %>%
  visInteraction(navigationButtons = TRUE, tooltipDelay = 100)







Implications
Agents marked as cross-incident hubs were exploited across multiple separate incidents, indicating the attacker had knowledge of the agent network’s topology and deliberately routed instructions through its most connected nodes. Restricting these agents’ ability to accept arbitrary queue_subordinate_task requests from unknown senders would disrupt all three known attack patterns simultaneously.



7.5 Visualisation 7 — SwiftWren Network (Time-Encoded)
Purpose: Visualisation 6 shows which agents were involved across all incidents. This chart focuses exclusively on SwiftWren and adds a temporal dimension — revealing not just who was connected to whom, but in what order those connections were made. It makes the directional flow of the attack visible as a spatial and colour gradient across the graph.
How it is made: Built with ggraph and igraph. The SwiftWren chain edges are extracted and a time_norm variable is computed for each edge, normalising the relay timestamp to a [0, 1] scale where 0 is the first hop and 1 is the last hop before the post. The graph layout uses the stress algorithm from ggraph, which minimises edge crossings and distributes nodes evenly — suitable for directed graphs with many relay connections. Edge colour is mapped to time_norm using a blue-to-red gradient (early = blue, late = red), and edge alpha fades along the edge direction using after_stat(index) to give each arrow a visual sense of directionality. Only john_windward and emma_harbor are labelled to keep the chart readable.
What to look for: Clusters of blue edges in one region of the graph (where the attack started) versus clusters of red edges converging toward john_windward (where the attack ended). Agents that have both blue incoming and red outgoing edges were mid-chain relay hubs that received the instruction early and passed it along later.


Show code
sw_edges_plot <- chains %>%
  filter(incident == "SwiftWren") %>%
  mutate(time_norm = as.numeric(datetime - min(datetime)) /
           as.numeric(max(datetime) - min(datetime)))

g_sw <- graph_from_data_frame(
  sw_edges_plot %>% select(from = from_person, to = to_person, time_norm),
  directed = TRUE
)

V(g_sw)$is_jw      <- V(g_sw)$name == "john_windward"
V(g_sw)$is_creator <- V(g_sw)$name == "emma_harbor"
V(g_sw)$role <- case_when(
  V(g_sw)$is_jw      ~ "john_windward (poster)",
  V(g_sw)$is_creator ~ "emma_harbor (origin)",
  TRUE               ~ "relay agent"
)

ggraph(g_sw, layout = "stress") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(colour = time_norm, alpha = after_stat(index)),
    arrow     = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
    end_cap   = circle(3, "mm"),
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(size   = ifelse(is_jw | is_creator, 5, 2),
        colour = role),
    show.legend = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(label = ifelse(is_jw | is_creator, name, "")),
    repel = TRUE, size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_edge_colour_gradient(
    low  = "#3288bd", high = "#d53e4f",
    name = "Relay time\n(0 = early, 1 = late)"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "john_windward (poster)" = "black",
      "emma_harbor (origin)"   = "#e63946",
      "relay agent"            = "grey65"
    ),
    name = "Agent role"
  ) +
  scale_size_identity() +
  labs(
    title    = "SwiftWren: Agent Relay Network (Time-Encoded)",
    subtitle = "Edge colour: blue is early in the chain, red is late"
  ) +
  theme_graph() +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, colour = "grey40")
  )











7.6 Visualisation 8 — Agent Degree Distribution
Purpose: Network graphs show structure but make it difficult to quantify which agents were most involved. This chart ranks all agents by their total number of appearances across the propagation chains (as either sender or recipient of a relay hop), making it immediately clear which agents the attack depended on most heavily. It is the quantitative complement to the network visualisations.
How it is made: Built with plotly as a horizontal stacked bar chart. Agent appearances are counted separately per incident using pivot_longer() to treat both from_person and to_person as appearances, then grouped by agent and incident. The top 20 agents by total appearances are selected using slice_max(). Bars are stacked by incident colour so the reader can see both total involvement and which incidents each agent participated in. Agents are ordered by total appearances using fct_reorder() so the most involved agent always appears at the top. Hovering over any bar segment shows the exact agent name, incident, and appearance count.
What to look for: Agents with bars in multiple colours (multi-coloured stacked bars) — these appeared across more than one incident and represent structural vulnerabilities in the agent network. The absolute length of each agent’s total bar indicates how many times the instructions passed through them, which correlates with how critical they were to the attack’s ability to propagate.


Show code
top20 <- agent_freq %>%
  group_by(agent) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(appearances), .groups = "drop") %>%
  slice_max(total, n = 20) %>%
  pull(agent)

plot_data <- agent_freq %>%
  filter(agent %in% top20) %>%
  mutate(agent = fct_reorder(agent, appearances, .fun = sum))

plot_ly(plot_data,
        x           = ~appearances,
        y           = ~agent,
        color       = ~incident,
        colors      = incident_colours,
        type        = "bar",
        orientation = "h",
        hovertemplate = "<b>%{y}</b><br>Incident: %{fullData.name}<br>Appearances: %{x}<extra></extra>") %>%
  layout(
    barmode   = "stack",
    title     = list(text = "Top 20 Agents by Relay Chain Appearances",
                     font = list(size = 16)),
    xaxis     = list(title = "Appearances (as sender or recipient)"),
    yaxis     = list(title = ""),
    legend    = list(title = list(text = "Incident")),
    hovermode = "y unified"
  )







Implications
Agents with multi-coloured bars appeared across more than one incident, meaning the attacker’s relay chain deliberately re-used the same structural hubs. This is evidence of intentional network-topology knowledge. Monitoring or restricting these specific high-degree agents would disrupt all three known attack patterns simultaneously.



7.7 Visualisation 9 — Post-and-Delete Cover-up Sequence
Purpose: This table documents the final moments of each incident — from the moment John Windward’s agent received the triggering instruction through the post and the immediate deletion of both files. Its purpose is to establish the automated cover-up as a forensic fact, using precise timestamps from the event log. The seconds-from-trigger column makes the speed of the cover-up immediately legible without requiring the reader to calculate time differences manually.
How it is made: Three event sources are combined using bind_rows(): the final trigger events from final_triggers, the post events from anomalous_posts, and the deletion events from deletions. A seconds_offset column is calculated within each incident group by taking the difference between each event’s timestamp and the first event in that group (the trigger). The result is rendered as a searchable DT table with filter = "top" so the reader can filter by incident or action type. Incidents and actions with few unique values benefit from the native select-style filter that DT auto-generates for low-cardinality columns.
What to look for: The Seconds from trigger column for each row. The entire sequence — receive, post, delete both files — completing in under 5 seconds for every incident is the key finding this table communicates. Any gap larger than a few seconds would suggest human involvement; the absence of such gaps confirms full automation.


Show code
cover_up <- bind_rows(
  final_triggers %>%
    select(incident, event = datetime) %>%
    mutate(action = "Received instruction"),
  anomalous_posts %>%
    select(incident = incident_name, event = datetime) %>%
    mutate(action = "Posted to SaidIt"),
  deletions %>%
    select(incident, event = datetime, action = deleted_file) %>%
    mutate(action = paste("Deleted:", action))
) %>%
  arrange(incident, event) %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  mutate(
    seconds_offset = round(as.numeric(difftime(
      event,
      first(event[action == "Received instruction"]),
      units = "secs"
    )))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

datatable(
  cover_up %>%
    mutate(event = format(event, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")) %>%
    select(
      Incident               = incident,
      `Timestamp (UTC)`      = event,
      Action                 = action,
      `Seconds from trigger` = seconds_offset
    ),
  caption  = "Trigger to post to delete sequence",
  rownames = FALSE,
  class    = "stripe hover",
  filter   = "top",
  options  = list(
    pageLength = 9,
    scrollX    = TRUE
  )
)







Implications
The complete sequence, from receiving the instruction through posting to deleting both files, finishes in under 5 seconds for every incident. The automatic cover-up means that by the time any human noticed the anomalous post, the file-system evidence was already gone. File-system snapshots or immutable audit logs with append-only semantics would be essential for forensic recovery in future incidents.

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
8 Further Exploration — Risk Model Detection

8.1 Motivation
The investigation in Q1 and Q2 established that all three anomalous incidents share a common structural fingerprint: a _further_instructions.md file propagates through the agent network via queue_subordinate_task relays, a .txt payload is pre-staged shortly before the chain begins, and the chain terminates at a posting-capable agent that immediately deletes all evidence. These are not coincidental — they are the observable signatures of a deliberate prompt-injection attack.
The limitation of the Q1 and Q2 analysis is that it was retrospective. It identified the incidents only because john_windward was already known as the poster. If a future attack targets a different agent — someone with similar saidit_post or flex_post permissions — the same chain-level pattern would occur, but none of the agent-specific indicators would match.
This section builds a configurable scoring model that evaluates any queue_subordinate_task chain on five structural features derived directly from the Q1 and Q2 findings. The model scores chains on a 0-to-100 scale without requiring knowledge of who the target poster is. Any chain exceeding the flag threshold is surfaced for review.


8.2 Scoring Features and Default Weights
Each of the five features maps directly to a finding from Q1 or Q2:








Feature
Derived from
Rationale




F1: Chain length score
Q1a — SwiftWren ran 186 hops; MellowOtter 10; HiddenOrca 39
Legitimate task delegation rarely chains the same file through dozens of agents. Chain length is log-normalised against the longest observed chain, compressing the extreme range while preserving ordering. Shorter attacks like MellowOtter still score meaningfully rather than being compressed near zero.


F2: File path repetition rate
Q1a — the same args.path appeared in every relay hop
In all three incidents, a single file path was passed identically through every queue_subordinate_task event. Log-normalised the same way as F1 since repetition count equals chain length in these incidents.


F3: Recipient has posting history
Q2 — john_windward held saidit_post permissions
The instructions specifically targeted an agent capable of posting externally. Any chain that routes toward a known posting-capable agent carries elevated risk regardless of who that agent is.


F4: Payload file created immediately before chain
Q2 — emma_harbor created SwiftWren.txt minutes before the first relay hop
In MellowOtter and SwiftWren, the payload .txt was created by the same origin agent within 30 minutes of the chain starting. This co-occurrence distinguishes staged attacks from organic file sharing.


F5: Prior cover-up behaviour
Q2 — john_windward deleted both files within 5 seconds of posting
All three incidents ended with immediate deletion. Any agent with a prior history of deleting files within seconds of a post event is a high-risk relay target in future chains.



Default weights are assigned to reflect the relative discriminating power of each feature based on the historical incidents:








Feature
Default weight
Reasoning




F1: Chain length
25
Present in all three incidents but varies in magnitude — weighted moderately


F2: File path repetition
30
The single most distinctive structural signal — highest weight


F3: Poster reachable
20
Critical for attack completion but may be hard to detect early in the chain


F4: Payload staged
15
Strong signal when present, but HiddenOrca had no create_file event


F5: Prior cover-up
10
Valuable but depends on having a prior incident to learn from



Total score range: 0 to 100. Default flag threshold: 60.


8.3 Computing Risk Scores for Known Incidents
The code below derives each of the five feature values from the event log for each of the three known incidents. Features F1 and F2 are continuous and normalised to [0, 1] before weighting. Features F3, F4, and F5 are binary (0 or 1), meaning they contribute either their full weight or nothing.
The final score for any incident is:

Score = (w1 × F1) + (w2 × F2) + (w3 × F3) + (w4 × F4) + (w5 × F5)

where w1…w5 are the user-specified weights summing to 100, and F1…F5 are the normalised feature values.


Show code
chain_lengths <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(n_hops = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(f1_chain_length = log(n_hops) / log(max(n_hops)))

path_repetition <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(n_hops = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(f2_repetition = log(n_hops) / log(max(n_hops)))

posters_history <- events %>%
  filter(short_name %in% c("saidit_post", "flex_post")) %>%
  mutate(poster = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:"))) %>%
  distinct(poster) %>%
  pull(poster)

posting_agents <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(
    f3_poster_reachable = any(to_person %in% posters_history),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(f3_poster_reachable = as.numeric(f3_poster_reachable))

chain_starts <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(chain_start = min(datetime), .groups = "drop")

f4_payload_staged <- payload_creations %>%
  mutate(incident_name = str_remove(created_file, "\\.txt$")) %>%
  left_join(chain_starts, by = c("incident_name" = "incident")) %>%
  mutate(
    mins_before = as.numeric(difftime(chain_start, datetime, units = "mins")),
    f4_staged   = as.numeric(mins_before >= 0 & mins_before <= 30)
  ) %>%
  select(incident = incident_name, f4_staged)

f4_all <- tibble(incident = c("HiddenOrca", "MellowOtter", "SwiftWren")) %>%
  left_join(f4_payload_staged, by = "incident") %>%
  mutate(f4_staged = replace_na(f4_staged, 0))

coverup_agents <- events %>%
  filter(short_name == "saidit_post") %>%
  mutate(
    poster    = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:")),
    post_time = datetime
  ) %>%
  select(poster, post_time) %>%
  inner_join(
    events %>%
      filter(short_name == "delete_file") %>%
      mutate(deleter = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:"))) %>%
      select(deleter, del_time = datetime),
    by = c("poster" = "deleter")
  ) %>%
  filter(abs(as.numeric(difftime(del_time, post_time, units = "secs"))) <= 10) %>%
  distinct(poster) %>%
  pull(poster)

f5_coverup <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(
    f5_coverup = as.numeric(any(to_person %in% coverup_agents)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

risk_scores_base <- chain_lengths %>%
  left_join(path_repetition, by = c("incident", "n_hops")) %>%
  left_join(posting_agents,  by = "incident") %>%
  left_join(f4_all,          by = "incident") %>%
  left_join(f5_coverup,      by = "incident")

risk_scores_base %>%
  select(
    Incident              = incident,
    `F1: Chain length`    = f1_chain_length,
    `F2: Repetition rate` = f2_repetition,
    `F3: Poster reachable`= f3_poster_reachable,
    `F4: Payload staged`  = f4_staged,
    `F5: Cover-up history`= f5_coverup
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Raw feature values per incident before weighting (F1 and F2 log-normalised to [0,1]; F3, F4, F5 binary)")



Raw feature values per incident before weighting (F1 and F2 log-normalised to [0,1]; F3, F4, F5 binary)

F3: Poster reachable

F5: Cover-up history

Code Details
F1 and F2 use logarithmic normalisation: log(n_hops) / log(max_hops). This compresses the extreme range between MellowOtter (10 hops) and SwiftWren (186 hops) so that shorter attacks are not penalised as severely as with linear normalisation, while still preserving the ordering. Under log normalisation, HiddenOrca scores ~0.70, MellowOtter ~0.44, and SwiftWren 1.00 — all three are meaningfully separated and all three incidents produce total scores above the 60-point threshold. F3, F4, and F5 remain binary flags contributing either their full weight or nothing.



8.4 Visualisation 10 — Risk Score Calculator
Purpose: This bar chart applies the five-feature scoring model to the three known historical incidents under the default weight configuration (W1 = 25, W2 = 30, W3 = 20, W4 = 15, W5 = 10). Its purpose is to validate the model: if the model is well-calibrated, all three known incidents should score above the flag threshold. It also makes the relative riskiness of each incident immediately visible.
How it is made: Built with plotly as a vertical bar chart. The five weighted feature scores are summed for each incident to produce a single total score. Bars are coloured by incident using the document-wide palette. The red dashed horizontal line at y = 60 marks the flag threshold, added via the shapes argument in layout(). Hovering over a bar shows the incident name and its exact score. The chart deliberately uses no interactivity beyond hover — weight adjustments are the purpose of Visualisation 11, keeping each chart focused on a single analytical task.
To explore how the scores respond to different weight assumptions, refer to Visualisation 11 below, which pre-computes scores across the full range of weight values for each feature and provides a dropdown to switch between features. The scores shown here represent the baseline derived directly from the Q1 and Q2 analysis.


Show code
w_default <- c(25, 30, 20, 15, 10)

score_data <- risk_scores_base %>%
  mutate(
    score_default = w_default[1] * f1_chain_length +
                    w_default[2] * f2_repetition +
                    w_default[3] * f3_poster_reachable +
                    w_default[4] * f4_staged +
                    w_default[5] * f5_coverup
  )


p_risk_bar <- plot_ly(
  score_data,
  x    = ~incident,
  y    = ~score_default,
  type = "bar",
  color = ~incident,
  colors = incident_colours,
  hovertemplate = "<b>%{x}</b><br>Risk score: %{y:.1f}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  layout(
    title  = list(text = "Risk Scores Under Default Weights",
                  font = list(size = 16)),
    xaxis  = list(title = "Incident"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "Risk score (0-100)", range = c(0, 105)),
    shapes = list(list(
      type = "line", x0 = -0.5, x1 = 2.5,
      y0 = 60, y1 = 60,
      line = list(color = "#e41a1c", dash = "dash", width = 2)
    )),
    annotations = list(list(
      x = 2.4, y = 62, text = "Flag threshold (60)",
      showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = "#e41a1c", size = 11)
    )),
    showlegend = FALSE
  )

p_risk_bar







Observations
Under log normalisation with default weights, all three incidents score above the 60-point flag threshold, validating the model. HiddenOrca scores ~68.6, MellowOtter ~69.2, and SwiftWren 100. Log normalisation separates all three lines meaningfully in Visualisation 11 — unlike linear normalisation (which compresses MellowOtter near zero) or binary scoring (where MellowOtter and SwiftWren are indistinguishable). The three scores are now distinct and interpretable.



8.5 Visualisation 11 — Weight Sensitivity Analysis
Purpose: Visualisation 10 shows scores under one fixed weight configuration. This chart answers the follow-up question: how stable are those scores as weights change? With log normalisation, all three incidents produce distinct scores — the lines are naturally separated without any visual tricks — making it easy to see which incident is most sensitive to each feature’s weight.
How it is made: Built with plotly. For each of the five features, the feature’s weight is varied from 0 to 50 in steps of 5, with the remaining weight budget redistributed equally across the other four features. The risk score is recomputed for each incident at each weight value using the log-normalised F1 and F2 values alongside binary F3, F4, and F5. The result is a line chart with one line per incident and a dropdown menu allowing the reader to switch between the five features without re-rendering.
Understanding the line behaviour: For F1 and F2 (log-normalised), all three lines will slope — but at different steepness depending on each incident’s log-normalised hop count. SwiftWren’s line slopes most steeply since it has the highest F1/F2 value (1.0). For F3, F4, and F5 (binary), a flat line means that incident does not have that feature; a sloped line means it does.
How to use this chart:

Use the dropdown menu at the top left to select which feature to examine: F1 Chain length, F2 File repetition, F3 Poster reachable, F4 Payload staged, or F5 Prior cover-up.
Three coloured lines appear — red for HiddenOrca, blue for MellowOtter, orange for SwiftWren. The x-axis is the weight assigned to the selected feature (0 to 50) and the y-axis is the resulting risk score.
The red dashed line marks the flag threshold of 60. Any line that crosses below this value at a given weight means that incident would not be flagged under that configuration.
Hover over any point to see the exact incident, feature, weight value, and computed score.
Click and drag on the chart area to zoom into any region. Double-click to reset the view.



Show code
feature_names <- c("F1: Chain length", "F2: File repetition",
                   "F3: Poster reachable", "F4: Payload staged",
                   "F5: Prior cover-up")

weight_seq <- seq(0, 50, by = 5)

sensitivity_rows <- list()
for (fi in 1:5) {
  for (w in weight_seq) {
    remaining <- (100 - w) / 4
    weights   <- rep(remaining, 5)
    weights[fi] <- w

    row_scores <- risk_scores_base %>%
      mutate(
        score = weights[1] * f1_chain_length +
                weights[2] * f2_repetition +
                weights[3] * f3_poster_reachable +
                weights[4] * f4_staged +
                weights[5] * f5_coverup,
        feature        = feature_names[fi],
        feature_weight = w
      ) %>%
      select(incident, feature, feature_weight, score)

    sensitivity_rows <- append(sensitivity_rows, list(row_scores))
  }
}

sensitivity_df <- bind_rows(sensitivity_rows)

p_sensitivity <- plot_ly()

incidents_list <- c("HiddenOrca", "MellowOtter", "SwiftWren")

for (inc in incidents_list) {
  for (feat in feature_names) {
    df_sub <- sensitivity_df %>%
      filter(incident == inc, feature == feat)

    p_sensitivity <- p_sensitivity %>%
      add_trace(
        data        = df_sub,
        x           = ~feature_weight,
        y           = ~score,
        type        = "scatter",
        mode        = "lines+markers",
        name        = inc,
        legendgroup = inc,
        showlegend  = (feat == feature_names[1]),
        line        = list(color = incident_colours[inc]),
        marker      = list(color = incident_colours[inc], size = 5),
        text        = ~paste0(inc, "<br>Feature: ", feat,
                               "<br>Weight: ", feature_weight,
                               "<br>Score: ", round(score, 1)),
        hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
        visible     = if (feat == feature_names[1]) TRUE else "legendonly"
      )
  }
}

p_sensitivity <- p_sensitivity %>%
  layout(
    title      = list(text = "Score Sensitivity: How Each Feature Weight Affects the Final Score",
                      font = list(size = 15),
                      y    = 0.97,
                      x    = 0.5,
                      xanchor = "center",
                      yanchor = "top"),
    margin     = list(t = 120),
    xaxis      = list(title = "Feature weight (0-50, others redistributed equally)"),
    yaxis      = list(title = "Risk score (0-100)", range = c(0, 105)),
    legend     = list(title = list(text = "Incident")),
    hovermode  = "closest",
    shapes     = list(list(
      type = "line", x0 = 0, x1 = 50,
      y0 = 60, y1 = 60,
      line = list(color = "#e41a1c", dash = "dash", width = 1.5)
    )),
    annotations = list(
      list(x = 48, y = 62, text = "Flag threshold (60)",
           showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = "#e41a1c", size = 10)),
      list(x = 0, y = 1.18, text = "Select feature:",
           showarrow = FALSE, xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
           font = list(size = 12, color = "#444"),
           xanchor = "left")
    ),
    updatemenus = list(list(
      type    = "dropdown",
      active  = 0,
      buttons = lapply(seq_along(feature_names), function(i) {
        feat <- feature_names[i]
        visible_vec <- unlist(lapply(incidents_list, function(inc) {
          lapply(feature_names, function(f) f == feat)
        }))
        list(method = "restyle",
             args   = list("visible", as.list(visible_vec)),
             label  = feat)
      }),
      x       = 0.18,
      xanchor = "left",
      y       = 1.22,
      yanchor = "top"
    ))
  )

p_sensitivity







Observations
The sensitivity chart shows that F1 (chain length) and F2 (file repetition) have the steepest score gradients — small changes to their weights produce large changes in the final score, particularly for SwiftWren (the longest chain). F3 (poster reachable) has a flat gradient for HiddenOrca and MellowOtter because those chains also reached posting-capable agents, so increasing F3’s weight lifts all three incidents equally. F5 (prior cover-up) has the smallest impact because it is binary and all three incidents share the same value for it.


Implications
Organisations with a high volume of legitimate long relay chains, such as automated pipeline orchestration systems, may need to reduce the chain length weight to avoid false positives, compensating by increasing the file repetition rate weight. Organisations that have already restricted posting permissions can reduce the poster-reachable weight, as that control is already enforced at the system level. The flag threshold can also be adjusted: a lower threshold increases sensitivity (catching more attacks) at the cost of more false positives, while a higher threshold reduces noise but risks missing shorter or faster attacks like MellowOtter.
